title: The Man Who Sold the Eiffel Tower
sources: The Hustle, 'The con man who sold the Eiffel Tower - twice' (May 1925; Lustig read that the tower was expensive to keep up; forged Ministry of Posts and Telegraphs letterhead; posed as deputy director general; met five scrap dealers at the Hotel de Crillon, Place de la Concorde; 1.2m-franc contract plus a 70,000-franc bribe; fled by train to Vienna; Poisson was too embarrassed to alert the police; a second sale followed and its mark reported it)

Yahoo / Smithsonian + Mental Floss summaries, 'How Victor Lustig Convinced a Paris Dealer to Buy the Eiffel Tower' (roughly 7,000 tons of scrap metal; dealers invited to the Hotel de Crillon; Poisson a newcomer to Paris who wanted to join the city's business circles; Lustig bet Poisson would be too embarrassed to go to the authorities)

El Pais English, 'The incredible story of the man who sold the Eiffel Tower (twice)' (in 1925 the tower was an expensive burden for the city, not yet the revered symbol; Lustig hired a forger for letterheads and seals and rented a suite at the Crillon; after the second attempt the mark went to the police and Lustig escaped and fled)
Today I Found Out, 'The Man Who Sold the Eiffel Tower' (money changed hands before Lustig vanished; Poisson, new in town and wanting a reputation, let it slide)

lines.text: In 1925, a con man
sold the Eiffel Tower.
To a real scrap metal dealer,
for a fortune.
See, Victor Lustig read in the papers
that Paris couldn't afford the tower anymore.
So he forged government letterheads.
He invited five scrap dealers to the fanciest hotel in Paris,
and swore them all to secrecy.
The city was selling the tower for scrap,
lines.caps: The city | was selling | the tower | for scrap,

lines.text: seven thousand tons of metal.
The bids came in,
but one name stood out.
Andre Poisson, a nobody dying to make his name.
lines.caps: Andre Poisson, | a nobody | dying to | make his name.

lines.text: He won the tower,
then paid a fat bribe on top,
just to make the deal go through.
The next morning, Lustig was on a train to Vienna,
and Poisson never called the police.
lines.caps: and Poisson | never called | the police.

lines.text: Too embarrassed to say he'd bought the Eiffel Tower.
Then Lustig came back for round two,
but that mark called the cops,
and Lustig vanished to America.
And the tower?
Still standing.
